issue.issue_text: Whether Section 295A of the I.P.C. would get attracted to the obtaining fact situation.

facts: An FIR was filed under Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) against the actor, producer, and director of a movie.

The complaint alleged that the picturization of a song, 'Manikya Malaraya Poovi', was blasphemous and offended the sentiments of the Muslim community, specifically focusing on a 'wink' by the actress.
The petitioners contended that the song is a traditional Muslim folk song from the Malabar region of Kerala that has been popular since 1978.
The song was released on YouTube as a promotional video for the movie.
law: Section 295A of the IPC criminalizes acts committed with the "deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings" of any class of citizens by insulting their religion or religious beliefs.

Citing the precedent in *Ramji Lal Modi*, the Court emphasized that Section 295A only penalizes insults that are perpetrated with deliberate and malicious intent, not those made unwittingly or carelessly.
The provision is intended to penalize activities that have a tendency to cause public disorder.
application: The Court analyzed the specific act in question—the picturization of the song featuring a 'wink'—and found that it did not constitute an insult or an attempt to insult the religion or religious beliefs of any class of citizens.

It found no evidence of a "calculated tendency" or a "deliberate and malicious intention" on the part of the petitioners to outrage religious feelings or disturb public order, which is a mandatory requirement to attract Section 295A.
The Court also characterized the person who filed the FIR as an "enthusiast" trying to "gain a mileage," suggesting the complaint was unwarranted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the picturization of the song did not meet the essential criteria for an offense under Section 295A of the IPC, as there was no deliberate and malicious intent to outrage religious feelings. Therefore, the Court held that the provision was not attracted to the facts of the case and quashed the FIR.

cases.case_name: Ramji Lal Modi v. State of U.P.
cases.principle: Section 295A of the IPC is constitutionally valid as it is a law imposing reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. The provision only punishes the aggravated form of insult to religion when perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging religious feelings, the calculated tendency of which is to disrupt public order.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An offence of insulting religion is only constituted by an aggravated form of insult which is perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of a class; acts that do not meet this standard are not punishable.
obiter: The calculated tendency of an aggravated form of religious insult is to disrupt public order, and a law penalizing such activity is a reasonable restriction on the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.
Laws creating offences relating to religion can be enacted in the interests of public order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that Section 295A of the I.P.C. does not apply to the facts of the case. By citing the Constitution Bench decision in Ramji Lal Modi v. State of U.P., the court reaffirmed that the provision only penalizes an "aggravated form of insult to religion when it is perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of that class." By quashing the F.I.R., the court implicitly concluded that the picturization of the song did not meet this high threshold of deliberate and malicious intent required to constitute an offense under the section.
legal_tests_applied: To attract Section 295A, the act must not be a mere insult to religion offered unwittingly or carelessly, but must be an "aggravated form of insult" perpetrated with the "deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of that class."

A law penalizing activities that have a "calculated tendency... to disrupt the public order" is a reasonable restriction on the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the petitioner's position by applying the strict interpretation of Section 295A laid down by the Constitution Bench in Ramji Lal Modi v. State of U.P., which requires a 'deliberate and malicious intention' to outrage religious feelings.
The court emphasized that Section 295A only punishes the 'aggravated form of insult to religion,' implying that the picturization of the song in the present case did not rise to that level.

The court noted that the language of Section 295A is not wide enough to cover restrictions outside the limits of constitutionally permissible legislative action, thereby reinforcing that the provision must be construed narrowly to protect the fundamental right to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reinforces the constitutional balance between the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and the state's power to impose reasonable restrictions in the interests of public order under Article 19(2).

The court affirmed that Section 295A must be interpreted strictly to ensure it is not applied for purposes not sanctioned by the Constitution, thereby preventing its misuse to stifle expression that does not have a calculated tendency to disrupt public order.
